title: 2026 Midterm Election Forecasts
text:
Status: Complete; post-election scoring in progress | Collaborators: Team 5, UMass Amherst DACSS | Methods: Bayesian poll aggregation, Monte Carlo simulation, calibration on past midterms | Tools: Python, R | Code: public on GitHub
Forecasts of the 2026 U.S. Senate and House elections, each run has 100,000 simulations that blend VoteHub polling, partisan-lean fundamentals, and Kalshi prediction-market prices. The Senate model was built with Team 5 in UMass Amherst’s DACSS program, chosen from seven competing versions we built and tested against one another and calibrated against more than two decades of historical polling misses. I extended it on my own into a district-by-district House model covering all 435 seats, recalibrated on the 2018 and 2022 midterms. Both models ran on a schedule every three hours through the final week and made their last call at 9:00 AM on Election Day.

title: Epstein Email Network
text:
Project summary
This ongoing project maps the social network embedded in the released Epstein corpus from the Epstein Transparency Act. A custom Python pipeline extracts email headers from roughly 1.4 million released email records, using a Mask R-CNN model to detect redactions and dual OCR engines to recover text, before a multi-pass name resolution process in R consolidates senders and recipients into a clean longitudinal network of 990 individuals across 21 time periods. The network is then modeled using Bootstrapped Temporal Exponential Random Graph Models (BTERGM) to test two hypotheses drawn from the literature on gender and social capital. Research Questions: (1) Do ties form disproportionately between individuals of the same sex? (2) Are women more likely to occupy brokerage positions, as measured by lagged Burt’s constraint? Results support sex-based homophily in tie formation and offer weak support for the brokerage hypothesis-women exhibit marginally lower constraint (i.e., are slightly more broker-like), though the effect is small. A notable secondary finding is an asymmetric sex pattern in tie formation: men initiate fewer ties but receive more. This work was completed in collaboration with Boaz Alkalay and Elizabeth Miller.

title: Epstein Email Network
text:
Analysis
The Department of Justice’s release of the Epstein records1 offers a rare chance to observe an elite communication network directly rather than through court testimony or journalistic reconstruction. With two collaborators, I built a Python pipeline that extracts headers from roughly 1.4 million released email records - classifying pages with dual OCR engines, locating redactions with a fine-tuned Mask R-CNN, and recovering sender and recipient fields - then resolved names in R through a six-pass matching pipeline (exact, substring, middle-initial, reversal, Jaro-Winkler fuzzy, and curated regex) into a longitudinal directed network of 990 confirmed unique individuals across 21 yearly waves, 2000–2020 (6,250 unique communication ties). Two hypotheses drawn from the literature on brokerage and gendered social capital2 structure the analysis: H1, that actors in structural brokerage positions - operationalized as low lagged Burt’s constraint3 - are disproportionately active in tie formation, with a supplementary question of who occupies those positions; and H2, that ties form disproportionately between individuals of the same sex.















The pooled network shows the classic core–periphery shape of an ego-anchored corpus: a dense communicative core surrounded by hundreds of low-degree contacts. Nodes are colored by sex; all names and identifying labels are deliberately withheld - the analysis concerns the structure of the network, not the identification of individuals. Activity is far from uniform in time: the network is sparse before Epstein’s 2008 plea agreement and peaks between roughly 2013 and 2018, which motivates estimating the final model on the 2009–2019 window rather than the full panel.








A descriptive first pass at H2: row-normalizing ties by sender sex shows how each group distributes its emails across recipient sexes. Descriptives like this cannot distinguish genuine homophily from confounding structure - reciprocity, degree heterogeneity, and the strong tendency of past ties to persist all shape raw same-sex proportions - which is exactly what the temporal ERGM below is for.

title: Epstein Email Network
text:
Modeling Tie Formation Over Time
Because ties are interdependent - an email begets a reply, shared contacts beget introductions - standard regression is inappropriate. We instead estimate a Bootstrapped Temporal Exponential Random Graph Model (btergm)4 on the 2009–2019 window, with structural controls for reciprocity, geometrically weighted degree distributions, transitive closure (GWESP), a linear time trend, and a one-year tie-memory term (R = 1,000 bootstrap resamples). H1 enters as sender- and receiver-side effects of Burt’s constraint, computed on the prior year’s network so the predictor is not endogenous to the ties being modeled; H2 enters as a same-sex match term alongside sender and receiver sex main effects. Out-of-sample tie prediction is strong (ROC AUC = 0.932 vs. a 0.51 random baseline; precision–recall AUC = 0.731 vs. 0.001), though a substantial share of that performance is carried by the memory term - persistence, not novelty, dominates elite email networks.















H1 is supported. A one-unit increase in constraint cuts the odds of receiving a tie by 74.4% (OR = 0.26, 95% CI [0.12, 0.30]) and of sending one by 71.8% (OR = 0.28, 95% CI [0.17, 0.34]) - low-constraint brokers are the network’s most active participants. H2 is supported. Same-sex dyads are 15.7% more likely to form a tie than mixed-sex dyads (OR = 1.16, 95% CI [1.10, 1.21]), net of reciprocity (OR = 176.57), popularity, transitivity, and tie persistence (memory OR = 5.09). The sex main effects reveal an unhypothesized asymmetry: male senders are 25.1% less likely to initiate a tie (OR = 0.75), while male receivers are 15.8% more likely to receive one (OR = 1.16) - women disproportionately write, men are disproportionately written to.








H1’s supplementary question - who occupies the brokerage positions? Burt’s constraint is bounded on [0, 1]: high values mean an ego’s contacts are densely interconnected (little brokerage opportunity), low values mark brokers bridging otherwise disconnected groups. Because the outcome is bounded, it is modeled with a beta regression (logit link) rather than OLS, whose residual diagnostics failed here - a specification choice that materially changed the conclusion. Controlling for year fixed effects among active nodes, men have significantly higher constraint than women (β = -0.018, 95% CI [-0.104, 0.068], z = -0.42), meaning women disproportionately occupy the broker-like positions - though the gap is modest in practical terms (about 0.02 SD).















The picture that emerges is of an elite network whose most active participants are its brokers, that clusters strongly by sex in who talks to whom, and in which women both initiate more communication and - modestly - occupy more of the structurally advantageous positions. Three caveats travel with these results: the corpus is the product of a federal investigation and is therefore an inherently selected sample of the true communication network; predictive performance leans heavily on tie persistence; and an MCMC-based mtergm robustness check proved computationally infeasible at this network size, leaving coefficient stability across bootstrap seeds as the primary robustness evidence. Full details, diagnostics, and replication materials are available upon request via the Contact page.

text: Status: Complete | Course: DACSS 603 (Statistics) final project | Methods: nested logistic regression, state-clustered standard errors | Data: Correlates of War, V-Dem | Tools: R

title: Deterrence and Interstate Conflict
text:
Project summary
This project examined deterrence theory using state-year data from the Correlates of War (COW) and Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) projects. Deterrence theory posits that States with greater military capability are less likely to be attacked and, therefore, to participate in conflict. This is closely related to Realist theories, which argue that the distribution of relative power in the international system is the primary influence on the probability of conflict. This yields a straightforward, testable hypothesis: as military capability increases, does the probability of participation in interstate conflict decrease? Research Question: Does greater military capability reduce the probability that a state participates in interstate conflict?

title: Deterrence and Interstate Conflict
text:
Analysis
Full write-up: Deterrence Project (Full Project Analysis)
Deterrence theory predicts that states with greater military capability should be attacked less often, and therefore participate in less conflict. As part of my graduate coursework I tested this against 14,634 state-years spanning 1870–2014, combining the Correlates of War project’s conflict and material capabilities data1 with the Varieties of Democracy project’s liberal democracy index2. Military capability is measured by the Composite Index of National Capability (CINC), a 0–1 index aggregating military, demographic, and industrial resources. Conflict is rare-only 3.98% of state-years involve participation-which shapes every modeling decision that follows.















Every key variable shifts substantially across the two-century span. Conflict rates spike around the World Wars and decline after the Cold War, democracy rises sharply after 1990, and average capability tracks the rise and fall of major powers. These trends are why year enters every model as a control: trade alone correlates with year at r = 0.66, so without the control other predictors would absorb temporal drift.








Grouping state-years by capability quartile previews the central finding: conflict participation rises with military capability-the opposite of the deterrence prediction. States in the highest CINC quartile participated in conflict in 8.64% of state-years, versus 0.36% for the lowest quartile. Notably, the pattern holds even for defenders: more capable states are attacked more, not less.
















Testing Deterrence Formally
Three nested logistic regressions estimate conflict participation: a bivariate baseline (CINC only), a controlled specification adding log-trade, democracy, log-population, and year, and a full model adding a centered democracy × trade interaction to test the liberal peace thesis. Because the same states are observed repeatedly, standard errors are clustered by state. The likelihood ratio test favors the interaction model (χ² = 5.09, p = 0.0241) and AIC agrees (4454.1 vs 4457.2), but BIC penalizes the extra parameter (4507.3 vs 4502.8) and the interaction fails under clustering-so the simpler controlled model is preferred for inference, with the full model shown below as the most complete specification.















CINC is positive and strongly significant (z = 3.11, p = 0.00186)-the null is rejected, but in the direction opposite the deterrence prediction. The full-range odds ratio (281) is misleading since no state traverses the whole 0–1 scale; a one-standard-deviation increase in CINC corresponds to an odds ratio of 1.2. Trade is protective (OR below 1), population strongly aggravating, both consistent with the literature. Democracy and the democracy × trade interaction lose significance once within-state correlation is accounted for: the interaction is significant unclustered (p = 0.0259) but fails clustering (p = 0.333), so the liberal peace interaction is not supported here.

The role-specific models sharpen the story. Even restricted to whether a state is attacked, capability associates positively with conflict (defender β = 3.88, p = 0.126), though the estimate is imprecise. The aggressor coefficient (β = 6.23, p = 0.00675) is roughly 1.6 times larger and precisely estimated, pointing to conflict initiation as the dominant channel: hard power appears to enable force projection at least as much as it deters attack. Whether that reflects opportunity, selection into capability by conflict-prone states, deterrence operating at the dyadic rather than state level, or unresolved endogeneity is an open question-the full write-up linked above works through each mechanism, the model diagnostics, and cross-validated performance.

title: Constraining the Commander in Chief
text:
Research question
Does Congress constrain the President less on national-security laws, and how does this change when paired with periods of divided government? Most statutes give some power away from the legislature in the form of discretion to the executive; the real question is how much deference is given.

title: Constraining the Commander in Chief
text:
Theory
Delegation theory. Legislatures write tighter, more detailed statutes when they distrust the agencies that will carry them out.1 Huber and Shipan extend the argument and show that the text of statutes is where this control is often exercised.2
The two presidencies. Wildavsky argued that there are effectively two presidencies: one that gets its way on defense and foreign policy, and a much weaker one at home.3 Later work finds that the foreign-policy advantage is real but smaller and more conditional than Wildavsky claimed.4
Partisan checks on war powers. Howell and Pevehouse show that Congress does constrain presidents on military matters, and that it does so mainly when the opposition party controls it.5 That predicts the divided-government effect should be at least as strong in national-security law as anywhere else.



Table 1: Hypotheses

H2

H3

title: Constraining the Commander in Chief
text:
Data
The corpus is every public law enacted from the 103rd through the 118th Congress (1993 to 2025): 6,302 laws pulled from the Congress.gov API and GovInfo. After dropping ceremonial laws (e.g., post office naming) and a few others 4,684 laws remain, split into about 149,000 sections and appropriations accounts. Each unit is classified as national security or domestic, and each law is coded for if either house that passed said was the opposite party of the President.



Public laws per Congress in the corpus. Ceremonial namings are flagged from titles and never pulled.

title: About Me
text:
I view life as one long learning experience. I love gathering knowledge from all disparate fields of study, ranging from engineering to political science. As part of this, I cannot help but focus on uncovering the mechanisms that form our world before our very eyes. My aim is to become a researcher and professor of political science, incorporating data analytics with all its beauty to such a philosophical science.



While I love exploring all facets of political science, I find myself inevitably drawn to investigations of why wars start, end, or never begin; how the structure of legislatures shapes what they produce; how people experiencing homelessness navigate fragmented systems of care. I also find my drawn to quantitative investigations including advanced regression, network analysis, and machine learning.



Bachelor’s - Political Science, minor in Policy Studies, received 2024 from Montclair State University.
Began undergraduate study in engineering at Penn State (calculus, chemistry, physics) before transferring to Montclair State to study political science.

title: Welcome to some of my data visualization projects
text:
This page highlights my ability to design clear, professional, and analytically useful data visualizations.
The figures presented here are not intended solely as final results, but as demonstrations of methodological choices-such as data transformation, visual encoding, annotation, and layout-that support accurate interpretation and effective communication.
Together, these examples reflect my emphasis on clarity, accessibility, and reproducibility in data-driven work.

title: Welcome to some of my data visualization projects
text:
The Homelessness Crisis




Individual Emergency Shelter Beds Per Homeless Individual
When looking at emergency shelter capacity relative to the homeless population, clear regional disparities emerge. States shown in red face shortages, with fewer than one shelter bed per homeless individual, while blue states indicate relatively higher capacity. This visualization highlights structural differences in how states address homelessness and emergency housing needs. The data used for this visualization was gathered from HUD data1 and a yearly report created by the World Population Review.2 Note that the map displays the contiguous United States; Alaska and Hawaii are excluded.

title: Welcome to some of my data visualization projects
text:
The Medical Debt Crisis

Medicaid Adult Coverage Expansion and Debt
In this next section I will be investigating the differences in the COVID-19 Medicaid subsidies expansion and medical debt.

















This bar chart compares medical debt collection rates across U.S. states by Medicaid expansion status in 2023, using data from Medicaid.gov3 and The Commonwealth Fund4. States are grouped by expansion status and benchmarked against the national average.
States that did not expand Medicaid show higher rates of medical debt in collections relative to both the national average and expansion states. While this does not provide causal evidence, this figure provides a quick, illustrative snapshot that highlights disparities linked to health care access and motivates deeper policy analysis.

title: Welcome to some of my data visualization projects
text:
Do We Respect Our Elders?
As the average American ages, increased expenditures into elderly care have been experienced. But this raises the question, what is our care capacity and what are our healthcare outcomes?

General Population Trends
Before tackling if an elder care crisis exists, one must first ask, what have the general population trends been in the United States.









































These three plots demonstrate how the American population has been aging nearly continuously since 1850. The median age has increased from 18.9 to 39.1 years between 1850 and 2024. Further sections will investigate how an aging population has created areas of policy innovation and policy failure. For example, do we have the infrastructure to care for more elders with fewer workers? The data for these three plots were obtained from the US Decennial Census5 via the IPUMS USA database6.

title: Welcome to some of my data visualization projects
section: How Does High Office Affect Wealth?
text:
How Does High Office Affect Wealth?
By virtue of studying political science, it is an inescapable truth that in our political-economic system power often acts as a wealth generation tool, and vice versa. This subsection will mostly look at wealth and power relying on public data.




My first question when thinking about how power may be translated into wealth is how individual presidents may have grown this wealth in office. While this graph may look clean and authoritative, there are several challenges that came in procuring the data. The main issue with the data is that the wealth start and end figures are calculated estimates sourced from the USOGE.7 What is interesting to see is that, at first brush, there are large percentage swings-but these largely reflect each president’s starting wealth: modest absolute gains appear enormous when starting wealth is small, while billion-dollar fortunes can swing sharply on valuation alone. Note that figures for the current administration are projections rather than final estimates.

title: Economic Dependence and UN Voting Alignment with China
text: Status: Complete | Course: DACSS 611 (Introduction to Python) final project | Methods: two-way fixed effects (PanelOLS), clustered standard errors, nested likelihood-ratio tests | Tools: Python (pandas, linearmodels) | Code: available on request

title: Economic Dependence and UN Voting Alignment with China
text:
Research question
Does economic dependence on China predict how countries vote with China in the UN General Assembly, and if so, does trade or investment/debt better explain the effect?
Two competing stories from IR theory make different predictions:

Liberal interdependence: economic ties create mutual interest and institutional forms pull countries together, therefore, deeper trade with China should pull a country’s voting closer to China’s.

This also supports the idea of including measures on a countries specific regime type. I do so as controls, and for my own interest.

Patron-client / structural dependence: Alignment can be bought. What I believe matters the most is asymmetric leverage, or large investment stocks, loans, and especially financial distress that gives China additional leverage. If this were true, investment from China will be the primary predictors.

The primary goal is to see which form of power actually moves voting alignment once we hold each country and each year fixed. Evidence for liberal interdependence would be a positive trade effect; evidence for structural dependence would be a positive investment effect with trade washing out.

title: Economic Dependence and UN Voting Alignment with China
text:

The analysis joins five sources, each contributing one piece of the final tapestry:

title: Economic Dependence and UN Voting Alignment with China
text:
Approach
All five sources were cleaned to a common country-year key (a name normalizer plus per-source crosswalks), aggregated to the country-year level, and left-joined onto the UN voting data with row-count checks at every merge. Agreement with China is measured overall and on contested votes, at both the state-year and the vote level. Models use two-way fixed effects (country and year) so that identification comes from within-country change, with standard errors clustered by country (and two-way by country and resolution in the vote-level models). Trade and investment blocks are added in a nested ladder on a frozen sample and compared with likelihood-ratio tests and AIC, then checked against country-specific time trends and log-dollar specifications.



Within-country effects of trade (blue) and investment / debt (red) on contested-vote agreement, primary specification.

title: Economic Dependence and UN Voting Alignment with China
text:
Conclusion
What the evidence says. Descriptively, countries that receive Chinese investment vote with China far more often, and the gap is largest on exactly the contested votes where leverage should matter - a picture that looks quite a bit like structural dependence. But once each country and year is held fixed, that relationship largely disappears: within-country changes in either trade or investment dependence don’t reliably move contested-vote agreement, and the nested-ladder and country-trend checks don’t find a robust effect for either channel. Therefore, this design finds the China alignment gap to be mostly a between-country fact - about which countries are economically tied to China - rather than evidence that deepening ties pulls a country’s votes into agreement over time. That doesn’t cleanly confirm liberal interdependence or structural dependence; if anything it cautions that the cross-sectional correlation both theories would point to doesn’t survive a demanding within-country test or are there other confounders that are driving agreement.
Limits The outcome is a contested-vote agreement rate, an imperfect proxy for true ideological distance. Trade missingness was filled with zeros, making dealing with missingness impossible. The investment stock is monotonic, which makes within-country identification difficult. With more time, the next steps would be a proper ideal-point outcome, an event-study designed around the timing of major loans, and a trade measure that separates true zeros from unreported years. Even then, I dont believe that there will be a profound relationship, but it would be interesting to investigate further.

title: Forecasting Democratic Backsliding
text: Status: In progress (data layer built; pre-registration being finalized) | Course: DACSS 756 (Machine Learning) final project | Data: V-Dem v16, Episodes of Regime Transformation (ERT) v16 | Tools: Python, R | Code: available on request

title: Forecasting Democratic Backsliding
Forecasting Democratic Backsliding
text:
Research questions
RQ1. Can V-Dem warning signs forecast the onset of autocratization in democracies, and how fast does that skill decay with horizon?
RQ2. Do Paxton’s leading signs add forecasting information beyond the outcome’s own trajectory, especially at long horizons, while the outcome’s own components mainly add short-horizon “momentum”?
RQ3. Is breakdown predictable once an episode has begun, and do its drivers differ from the drivers of onset?

title: Forecasting Democratic Backsliding
text:
Design
The study is pre-registered before any model is fit: the panel, labels, and audits are built and tested first, a power simulation on synthetic labels sets the minimum effects worth reporting, and the final comparison is scored once on a locked test set. Models are compared against a persistence baseline using Brier skill and precision-recall AUC, with country-clustered bootstrap intervals and drop-group refits to measure what each family of warning signs adds.



Power simulation used to set minimum detectable effects before the pre-registration is frozen (synthetic labels only).

title: Forecasting Democratic Backsliding
text:
Results
Models are still being finalized and estimated. The results will be public soon.
The project grew out of an earlier study in the same course, which tested a fly-connectome reservoir on conflict forecasting: see Can a Fly Brain Forecast War?.

title: End-of-Life Planning Among Unsheltered and Unhoused Individuals
text:
Status: Planned (proposal written) | Methods: survey, semi-structured interviews | Output: research proposal (PDF)

This project aims to examine how unsheltered and unhoused individuals engage in end-of-life (EoL) planning, an area that remains largely overlooked in homelessness and public health research. By drawing on survey data and semi-structured interviews, the study will explore how shelter status, geographic mobility, and access to medical and legal resources shape attitudes toward and engagement with EoL planning. By distinguishing between unsheltered individuals and those who are unhoused but mobile (e.g., living in vehicles), the research aims to highlight how mobility and fragmented service systems can disrupt continuity of care and planning at life’s end. It is my hope the findings will inform more humane and effective policies within Continuums of Care, emphasizing the importance of aligning end-of-life decisions with individual wishes rather than structural constraints.

  Read the proposal (PDF)

title: Can a Fly Brain Forecast War?
text:
Question
Does the wiring of the Drosophila mushroom body, used as a fixed recurrent network (a reservoir), forecast armed conflict better than random networks and conventional models?

title: Can a Fly Brain Forecast War?
text:
Design
Monthly state-based conflict deaths (UCDP GED, country-month panel, 1989-2025) are forecast at horizons of 1, 3, 6 and 12 months. The reservoir is a leaky echo-state network wired as the fly’s mushroom body plus the olfactory projection neurons that feed it (FlyWire). In Tier 1 every connection is frozen and only a linear readout is trained, which is the cleanest test of whether the wiring itself helps. Control networks (weight-shuffled, degree-preserving rewired, random) get identical tuning budgets, validation uses five expanding-window rolling-origin folds, and 2021-2025 is held out as a locked test set.

title: Can a Fly Brain Forecast War?
text:
Findings
Conventional baselines. Ridge regression on 28 hand-built history features beats a tuned moving-average baseline by 1.6% to 4.7% in RMSE across horizons; random forest and gradient boosting never reliably beat ridge.

The reservoirs supply memory, but the fly’s wiring adds nothing. With history-free inputs, the reservoirs must create the memory themselves. Across horizons, the fly and its three control networks close 89% to 98% of the gap between ridge on current values and ridge on full history, and the fly is indistinguishable from the controls.









The mechanism is leaky averaging, not recurrence. Linear reservoirs do at least as well as nonlinear ones, a bank of unconnected leaky units ties every network, and plain exponential moving averages of the inputs land within rounding of the reservoirs. The 96 mushroom-body output neurons read out worse than 96 random units.

A fixed fly-connectome reservoir recovers nearly all the forecasting skill that explicit history provides, but so does a random network, a bank of unconnected leaky units, and a set of exponential moving averages.

title: Paterson City Mayor’s Office Collaboration
text:
Status: Complete (published) | Course: POLS 324: Advanced Public Policy Analysis (Spring 2024), Dr. Fanny Lauby | Recognition: Certificate of Recognition for Solving Authentic Complex Challenges (2024) | Collaborators: two Montclair State University peers; Paterson City Mayor’s Office | Output: white paper chapter (PDF)

As part of a white paper published by Montclair State University, two of my peers and I worked in close collaboration with the Paterson City Mayor’s Office to identify and develop solutions to an ongoing crisis in local emergency shelters. Local state law stipulates that the average length of stay in an emergency shelter must remain below a set number of days, but local shelters were not in compliance. We found that, by utilizing niche techniques ranging from merging Continuums of Care to modifying funding schemes, local emergency shelter conditions could be brought into compliance with New Jersey state law.

  Read the chapter (PDF)

This project was completed for Advanced Public Policy Analysis at Montclair State University in Spring 2024, taught by Dr. Fanny Lauby, and received the university’s Certificate of Recognition for Solving Authentic Complex Challenges.
